newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: Jospin seeks to quash French EMU doubts.
newsitem.headline: Jospin seeks to quash French EMU doubts.

text.p: French Prime Minister Lionel Jospin sought on Tuesday to quash doubts about his new left-wing government's commitment to joining a single European currency raised by a junior minister for Europe.

Jospin would not comment directly on remarks by European Affairs Minister Pierre Moscovici, which implied there was some doubt about whether France would join the euro, but he told a news conference at a European Union summit in Amsterdam he was totally committed to launching the single currency on time.
"On the conditions that I raised during the (election) political debate, I am totally in favour of the single currency, and of launching of the single currency on time," Jospin said.

Moscovici earlier prompted uncertainty about economic and monetary union for the second time in a week by saying in a radio interview that Paris would decide whether or not to join the euro after assessing public finances.
"We must asses the state of our public finances, and it will be in light of this situation that we will decide whether or not to move to the euro," Moscovici said.
After hours of uncertainty in financial markets, Jospin's spokesman Manuel Valls told reporters that Moscovici had spoken out of turn.
"He spoke too quickly. This is not an expression either of our political will or of a strategy," Valls said.
Jospin said he wanted the single currency not only because France had given its word but also because it could give Europe greater control over its monetary future and a more powerful world role.
"The euro is, I think, a stage towards the reconstruction of an international monetary system worthy of that name, which I think is necessary for the stability of world economic relations," he said.

The prime minister is due to deliver his government's keynote policy statement to parliament on Thursday and is expected to announce an audit of public finances to check how far France really is from the EMU target of limiting the overall deficit to three percent of gross domestic product.

The previous centre-right government defeated on June 1 had insisted that France was on target to meet the criterion, but Socialist officials have said the first indications they have received on tax revenues and welfare accounts suggest otherwise.

The Jospin government jolted France's EU partners last week by seeking a delay to study a controversial pact limiting budget deficits under EMU, and demanding that a resolution to promote growth and jobs be given equal weight.
Moscovici added to the shock at the time by saying he did not expect the government would approve the so-called stability pact at this week's Amsterdam summit.

Hours later, President Jacques Chirac made clear he wanted to reach a deal in Amsterdam, and Jospin indicated he would try to do so. The agreement was sealed on Monday after France's EU partners accepted a statement pledging greater efforts to boost growth and employment.
